names: why do we fall forward when a bus stops
subject: science

asks: A drawing of a coin resting on a card on top of a glass, and beside it the same glass after the card is flicked away sideways, the coin fallen into the glass.
A drawing of a toy cart carrying a wooden block, and beside it the same cart stopped suddenly against a book, with the block tipped forward and an arrow showing the cart's motion.
picture.why: The coin dropping straight into the glass shows an object staying where it was while the thing under it is pulled away.

big_idea.text: An object keeps doing what it is doing, staying still or moving straight at the same speed, until a force makes it change.

objectives.can: Predict what a resting or moving object does when the thing under it is suddenly moved
Explain why standing passengers fall backwards when a bus starts suddenly
Explain why the coin drops into the glass

why_it_matters.text: It explains why you lurch when a bus starts or stops, and why seat belts and helmets save lives.

the_why.text: Changing how something moves needs a push or a pull on it; a fast flick pulls the card away before it can drag the coin along, so the coin stays where it was and, with nothing under it, gravity pulls it straight down.

picture.text: A coin resting on a card on top of a glass. A finger flicks the card hard sideways: the card shoots away, and the coin stays in the same place for an instant, then drops straight down into the glass. A slow push is shown beside it: the card drags the coin off with it.
picture.standard: coin on a card on a glass (card flicked away)

card.diagram_ask: A drawing of a coin resting on a card on top of a glass, and beside it the same glass after the card is flicked away sideways, the coin fallen into the glass.

needs_first.text: A force is a push or a pull.
Friction is the force between two surfaces that rub.

mistakes.mistake: Moving things stop on their own because their push runs out.
mistakes.why_it_fails: A rolling ball stops because friction and air push against it; on a smoother floor it rolls much further.

mistakes.mistake: An object moves along with whatever it is resting on.
mistakes.why_it_fails: It moves only if a force acts on it; a fast flick gives the card almost no time to push the coin, so the coin stays.

mistakes.mistake: A force is needed to keep a thing moving at the same speed.
mistakes.why_it_fails: A force is needed only to change motion; with no friction a moving thing would go on for ever without one.

opening_question.question: A coin rests on a card on top of a glass. If you flick the card away very fast, where will the coin go?
opening_question.answer: Straight down into the glass: it stays where it was while the card is pulled away.

route.what: Show the coin on the card on the glass and ask where the coin will go when the card is flicked fast. Ask for a guess.
Flick the card: the card flies off and the coin drops straight into the glass.
Push the card slowly instead: the coin rides off with the card. Ask: what is different?
A slow push lets friction drag the coin along; a fast flick gives no time for that, so no force moves the coin sideways and it stays.
Name it inertia: a thing keeps doing what it is doing until a force changes it.
A bus starts suddenly: your feet move with the floor, but your body stays where it was, so you fall backwards.
A bus brakes suddenly: the learner predicts which way the passengers lean, and why, before it is shown.
Set the task: coin, card and glass at home.
The learner says why the coin falls into the glass.

questions.question: You flick the card from under the coin very fast. Where does the coin go?
options: It stops and floats where it was
questions.explain: No sideways force reaches the coin in that instant, so it stays put, and with the card gone gravity pulls it down.

questions.question: A bus starts suddenly. Which way do standing passengers lean?
options: Backwards, because their bodies stay where they were while their feet move forward
They do not move at all
questions.explain: The floor pulls the feet forward, but no force acts on the upper body at first, so it stays behind.

questions.question: A ball rolled on a floor slows down and stops. Why?
options: Friction from the floor and air pushes against it
Moving things always stop by themselves
questions.explain: A force is needed to change motion; friction is that force, and on a smoother floor the ball goes further.

try_it.title: Coin, card and glass
try_it.stands_for: The coin is the resting object; the card is what moves under it; the flick is a sudden pull.
try_it.predict: When you flick the card away fast, will the coin go with the card or fall into the glass?
steps: Put the card flat on top of the glass.
Place the coin in the middle of the card, over the mouth of the glass.
Flick the edge of the card hard and fast with your finger, sideways.
Set it up again and this time push the card slowly.
try_it.observe: With the fast flick the coin drops straight into the glass; with the slow push the coin moves off with the card.
try_it.question: Why does the coin fall into the glass when the card is flicked fast, but move with it when pushed slowly?
try_it.expected: Because a fast flick gives friction no time to pull the coin sideways, so the coin stays where it was and falls straight down, while a slow push lets friction drag it along.
try_it.write: A resting thing stays at rest until a force moves it. The fast flick gave no force to the coin, so it stayed and fell.
try_it.in_class: Pairs, one glass, card and coin each. The teacher draws the coin on the card on the glass on the board and asks for predictions before anyone flicks. Ask: why did the slow push take the coin along? A pair whose coin flew off flicked upward or too slowly.

leave_out: mass as the measure of inertia in numbers
